abstract: |
  Papers 2a and 2b changed the feature set and then the prediction
  objective for a conditional-logit model of UK All-Weather Flat
  handicaps. This paper holds both fixed and changes the function class
  instead, replacing the linear score with a gradient-boosted ensemble of
  decision trees fitted on the same depth-three Plackett–Luce likelihood,
  selected from a `r nrow(targets::tar_read(gbt_tuning_results)$all_results)`-point
  cross-validated grid on
  `r scales::comma(dplyr::n_distinct(targets::tar_read(gbt_train_data)$key$race_id))`
  training races. Scored on
  `r scales::comma(dplyr::n_distinct(targets::tar_read(gbt_test_data)$key$race_id))`
  held-out test races, the tree ensemble ranks no better than paper 2b's
  linear predictor: a paired bootstrap of the two models' P1_rank,
  Brier_place and pseudo-$R^2$ contains zero on every metric, despite the
  two being materially different models (within-race score correlation
  `r sprintf("%.3f", targets::tar_read(score_agreement_3_vs_2b)$pearson_r)`;
  a different top pick in
  `r scales::percent(1 - targets::tar_read(score_agreement_3_vs_2b)$share_same_top, accuracy = 1)`
  of races). Naive win-picking and single-bet betting value show the same
  pattern against both papers 2a and 2b. The market's own probabilities
  beat the tree ensemble decisively on both ranking metrics — the one
  contrast in the paper whose interval excludes zero — continuing the
  pattern of every paper in this series. Changing the function class does
  not close the gap the feature set and the objective also left open.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Paper 2a extended paper 1's feature set; paper 2b extended the objective
from predicting the winner to predicting the finishing order. This paper
holds both fixed and changes the function class instead: the linear score
of a conditional logit is replaced by an ensemble of decision trees,
fitted by gradient boosting on the same depth-three ranking likelihood
paper 2b uses. A tree finds interactions among features on its own,
rather than needing each one specified as a term in advance, and it is
the model class chosen specifically to admit going affinity — a horse's
own record on the going it faces today — without the explicit
interaction a linear model would need and paper 2b did without.

The three questions are the ones papers 2a and 2b ask, and the answer to
each is the same. **Q1 — ranking performance.** Does the tree ensemble
predict the finishing order better than paper 2b's linear model? It does
not: a paired bootstrap of the two models' ranking metrics on the same
test races contains zero on every metric compared, and the market's own
probabilities beat both. **Q2 — win-picking.** Does richer, data-found
interaction structure make it a better winner-picker than papers 2a or
2b? It does not: on the naive betting rule the point estimates run the
wrong way against both comparators, and the intervals do not distinguish
any of the three models. **Q3 — betting value.** Turned into a
single bet per race, does that reach a return paper 2b's own single-bet
rule does not already reach? It does not: win, place and each-way returns
overlap paper 2b's figures throughout.

The tree ensemble and the linear predictor are not the same model
reaching the same answer by default — they disagree on the top horse in a
third of test races — but they rank, pick and bet alike, and both lose to
the market by about the margin the series has shown throughout. What that
tie means, and what it does not settle, is taken up in @sec-discussion.

@sec-data sets out the shared data and feature set, including the
going-affinity feature this change of model class was chosen to
accommodate; @sec-method motivates the objective and the model class;
@sec-model describes the fit and how it was tuned; @sec-results answers
the three questions in order; and @sec-discussion draws the series'
three changes together.

# Acknowledgments {.unnumbered}

I have been interested in modelling horse racing since first
acquiring the Smartform database more than a decade ago. The project
has been picked up and put down many times, the obstacle almost
always being the gap between an idea and a running implementation.
What is different now is that working alongside Claude Code
(Anthropic's coding agent), with web-based Claude as a research
companion, has compressed that gap dramatically. I am grateful to
my brother, Michael Gillen, for the suggestion to build the model
on All-Weather races — the foundation of the scope choices set out
in @sec-data. The design choices — dataset, scope, model,
comparison, editorial line — are mine. The implementation, the bulk
of the draft prose, and a great deal of the verification were
Claude Code's, under my direction; every output was reviewed and
edited before it reached the paper. I do not yet know what general
lessons this experiment points to about the value of human–AI
collaboration in applied statistics. That uncertainty is part of
why I am doing the work, and these papers are partly a record of
that experiment.
